newsitem.title: RUSSIA: OSCE emphasis will change in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: OSCE emphasis will change in Chechnya.

text.p: The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe's new representative for Chechnya said on Monday he would not be mediating between Moscow and the region's separatists when he took up his post.
Moscow said on Friday it had called for the change in the OSCE's role at a meeting of the security forum's permanent council last month.

The OSCE played a key part in peace negotiations in Chechnya, helping to seal a deal last August ending 21 months of fighting between local rebels and Russian troops which had killed tens of thousands of people.

But while the mediation was welcomed by Aslan Maskhadov, the former separatist chief-of-staff elected president of the region in January, it was bitterly opposed by conservatives in Moscow who saw it as unnecessary interference by the West.
On Friday the Russian Foreign Ministry said there was no need for the OSCE to mediate in further negotiations on a political settlement of the conflict.
It should concentrate instead on monitoring human rights, helping to establish democratic institutions, the return of refugees and humanitarian aid, the ministry said in a statement.
Rudolf Thorning-Petersen, the Danish diplomat appointed last week to take over the OSCE's Grozny mission, said the change of emphasis did not contradict the OSCE's mandate.
"As the two parties are now in direct contact and negotiations there is no need or role for the OSCE in mediation... It is the priorities which have changed not the mandate as such," he said.
"The mandate is rather wide-scope, so it could include (mediation) once again, if the parties agree to that," he added, speaking by telephone from the Danish capital.
Officials in Maskhadov's entourage, who see OSCE mediation as an added lever in their negotiations with Moscow, were not immediately available for comment on the change.
Last week Maskhadov said the talks had hit a dead end.
The rebels, who forced Moscow to the negotiating table by humiliating its troops, insist they have won independence. But Moscow says Chechnya cannot leave the Russian Federation.
The August peace deal involved putting off a final decision on Chechnya's political status for five years.
But while an interim political deal remains unsigned, the shattered region is desperately short of funds to reconstruct ruined homes, schools, hospitals, farms and factories.
Russia's Nationalities Minister Vyacheslav Mikhailov said on Monday that Moscow should start paying out pensions and compensation to Chechnya before the two sides sign formal economic agreements.
"Sooner or later a package of agreements with Chechnya will be signed. But we need to start with little things," he told Interfax news agency.
Mikhailov disputed Maskahdov's assertion that the talks had foundered and that Moscow was holding the region to ransom.
"You just have to look at the initiatives coming from the federal centre for it to be clear that the negotiating process has not slowed down," Interfax quoted Mikhailov as saying.
Thorning-Petersen said he planned to go to Chechnya in mid-May to take over from Swiss diplomat Tim Guldimann, who has been in Chechnya since January 1996.
